lesson.title: The Mind's Small Workbench: Short-Term Memory
lesson.summary: Short-term memory is the limited-capacity, limited-duration store that holds information currently being attended to and used, serving as the workspace between fleeting sensory impressions and lasting long-term memory.
lesson.body:
Short-term memory is the second stage of the multi-store model, a limited-capacity, limited-duration workspace that holds whatever information a person is currently attending to and actively using. Unlike sensory memory, which briefly holds an almost complete record of raw sensory input, short-term memory holds only the small portion of that input attention has selected, and it holds even that small amount for a limited time. Psychologist George Miller's classic estimate held that short-term memory can hold about seven items, plus or minus two, though later research suggests the true capacity without any special strategy may be smaller, closer to around four meaningful units at a time.

The key to Miller's estimate is that the relevant unit is not necessarily a single digit or letter but a "chunk," a meaningful grouping of information treated as a single unit. This is why chunking, the strategy of organizing individual pieces of information into larger, familiar units, can dramatically increase how much information short-term memory can effectively hold. Six individual letters like F, B, I, C, I, A would ordinarily strain short-term memory's capacity, but grouped into the two familiar chunks "FBI" and "CIA," the same six letters become far easier to hold onto, since short-term memory is now working with two units instead of six.

Short-term memory is also limited in duration. Without some form of active maintenance, information held in short-term memory tends to fade within roughly twenty to thirty seconds. Classic research using distractor tasks, having people count backward or perform some other activity that prevents them from silently repeating information to themselves, shows just how quickly recall drops off once rehearsal is blocked. This rapid decay is part of why a phone number heard once can slip away entirely if a person is briefly interrupted before they have a chance to write it down or repeat it.

Keeping information active in short-term memory generally happens through rehearsal, and psychologists distinguish two kinds. Maintenance rehearsal is simple repetition, silently repeating a phone number over and over just to keep it available a little longer. Elaborative rehearsal instead connects new information to existing knowledge and meaning, thinking about how a new fact relates to something already known. Maintenance rehearsal can keep information alive in short-term memory for a while, but elaborative rehearsal is generally far more effective at eventually transferring that information into long-term memory, since it builds richer, more meaningful connections rather than just repeating a shallow trace.

Short-term memory's contents are inherited directly from sensory memory, specifically from whatever fraction of the sensory trace attention manages to select before it fades. Because sensory memory decays so quickly and holds so much raw information at once, short-term memory ends up working with an already heavily filtered, attention-selected slice of the original stimulus, which is one reason short-term memory's contents feel focused and manageable even though the sensory information they were drawn from was, for a brief moment, much richer and more complete.
